utterances.text: Well, there are some remarks here which should be by Karajko Ramo, and it says Karajko [phoen.], which was his real name. That was a mistake put right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the cinema you were registered by the Red Cross, were you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was before you went to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fact that you were secretly transferred cannot remain a secret, because you were registered in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. But we were transferred in the very early hours of the morning, around 5 a.m., which means, in practical terms, where nobody was able to see us being transferred to the chess club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sure you discussed this at length with the colleagues that shared your fate. And was it never mentioned that this transfer was organised in such a way precisely to protect you from the extremists in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Why? We were to have been released on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to know whether anyone had ever mentioned that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Kaonik, were you registered by the Red Cross as a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, several days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got an ID card to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We received a document, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that document state "prisoner of war"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Red Cross issued documents of this kind and certificates of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This morning, at the end of the examination-in-chief, you told us that members of the military police beat you up in the courtyard of the cinema. Were you born in Bukve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You complained to Santic, and he said that he would inform Cerkez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cerkez had his command in that building, did he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You mean where we were?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, that was where the military police unit was located, and I can only assume that the accused Cerkez was in the building as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the headquarters of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never heard what happened to the man who had attacked you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you claim that the man who attacked you was a member of the guard or did he come from outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. He was a member of the guard. And not only one person, but there were two of them, and both of them stood guard at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I have one more question to ask. You mentioned the intelligence officer, Dzenanovic Fadil, who gave you the information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a relation to Esad Dzenanovic, the commander of the Vitez army; that is to say, the 325th Mountain Brigade in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They have the same surname. Possibly they are related, but I couldn't say. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not sure.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to make matters quite clear, you say you are not from Bukve, but you are from Sadovace; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is a much more definite place, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it near Bukve, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, it is -- you can't see them geographically. They're not that close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one further question. The two soldiers that beat you up, did they not use words which you came to understand that one of these men's mothers had been killed on the previous day or that particular day, and that he was drunk, and that he found you and took it out on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, that's a contradictory statement. If he was drunk, he could not have stood guard, as we said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was nothing of that kind said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is the end of my cross-examination. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, for testifying. Cross-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. We're taking up a little time to prepare ourselves. My learned colleague Mr. Kovacic examined the subjects that I have prepared, but I shall try not to repeat what he has just asked, and I hope that I shall be brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. AC, let me introduce myself. My name is Mitko Naumovski. I'm an attorney from Zagreb and I'm one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Kordic. I'm going to ask you a few questions now. Mr. AC, you made a statement in 1994, at the Supreme Court in Zenica, as a witness. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, there were four formal statements to the OTP of this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the latest conversation you had a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. AC, you spoke today about your transfer from Vitez to Kaonik. For the first time, although you have given six statements to date, you say, during the examination-in-chief today, that a man named Marko told you that Mr. Kordic had some link -- was connected to your transfer in some way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I mentioned that particular man, Marko, in one or two other statements that I made previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But never in this context, in relation to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The statements that I made earlier on were broader in context and focused on the overall situation in the Vitez municipality, because I was not told in precise terms to mention any individuals who could come up in this trial, and to go into all the details and parameters related to those individuals. Had I known at the time that this would be required of me and that the accused Kordic would actually be accused and indicted, I would probably have mentioned that as a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, that particular individual named Marko, what duty did he perform at the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, according to the manner in which the other members of the HVO police behaved towards him, he gave the impression of being a sort of commander of theirs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In one of your statements, when you talked to the interviewers for several days, on 31st, 1996, January 1996, and later on, you said that Marko was the commander of the camp or prison. Was that that same Marko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know any other Markos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is your last sentence in that particular statement. So that is the only Marko that we're discussing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, do you know whether what Marko said was true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Marko told you; do you know whether that was true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Could you clarify that question? What do you mean, "what he said"? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Mr. Kordic had something to do with your transfer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his source of information was, where he came by that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, if I identified him as the commander of the camp or the leader, then this happened on the basis of the relationship of the other members of the HVO police who were in that particular camp. So I can only assume that the source of his information was from a very influential quarter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. That is your conclusion. But you have no actual knowledge about that? You saw no document to that effect or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We were not, of course, given any documents of that kind. We were just prisoners and waited for execution of some kind, to go trench digging. And we know that many people who went trench digging never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree with me that that is your own conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, it's not my conclusion, as I said a moment ago. That particular piece of information was unequivocally given out by Marko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But as to your conclusion as to his source of information, you have no actual factual evidence to bear that out, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that on that particular day, when we were exchanged, that they had indeed received some documents or telegrams, but of course I did not have any insight into that. The document -- I saw the documents from a distance; that is to say, I saw him carrying the document in his hand, but of course I did not know the contents of that document, nor could I see the contents of it. And I think that there were many documents. One of the documents, we signed our names and said that we were leaving the Kaonik camp on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't draw closer to the document. You didn't know who signed it, what stamp was on it, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have access to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I mentioned Kaonik, but you were not mistreated in Kaonik, were you, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, if you mean physical mistreatment, no, but I had other forms of trauma which are much worse than the one you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was what you said in one of your statements and I just repeated it, but, nevertheless, we can go forward.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were words contained in a statement and this is an actual trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have heard many witnesses in this courtroom who were transferred with you from Vitez to Kaonik. I don't wish to reveal a protected name, and so as to avoid repeating those names, but Their Honours are aware of them; none of them mention this allegation that you just made, that Mr. Kordic issued an order for your transfer from Vitez to Busovaca in the prison. Not one of those witnesses said that in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is quite possible, because, after all, we were assigned to different rooms, in small groups of a couple of men, and we had no communication amongst each other. So that it is quite possible that what you say is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, but you communicated with those people for years after the events. So many years have gone by, and none of them appeared to have learned certain details afterwards. And to this day, not one of them conveyed this allegation in this court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If what you are saying is true, that a certain number of witnesses who have passed through this courtroom did not mention this, I have already said that that is quite possible. Now, why they didn't have any such information, one can conclude from this that I had heard it. It is true that I did not pass this on to anyone. So if this information is important, no one could have learnt it from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted). I don't wish to repeat his name. I assume you know who I mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that I didn't discuss it with anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We can proceed to another topic. Mr. Cerkez's Defence asked you in detail about the meeting on the 19th of October, 1992. I have only a few relevant to that meeting. Where was the telephone set itself, in relation to the place where you were sitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The room was quite large. The telephone set, in relation to where I was sitting, was about a couple of metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So it was the traditional telephone set with a receiver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without a loudspeaker?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, without.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your earlier statements, and you repeated that yesterday or today, you said that on two occasions, through the conversation that Mr. Cerkez had with Mr. Kordic, and later on when (redacted) was speaking to him, that you heard the terms and conditions laid down by Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They could be heard -- they couldn't be heard directly while they were talking, but they were heard because they were repeated by the people at the other end holding the receiver. So we heard what this person was repeating regarding the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But when you made your statement on the 4th of September, '95, you said, explicitly, that during the conversation that you heard Mr. Kordic saying these things and setting the terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. A part of that conversation was carried out in a way that the accused, Kordic, was, one could say, hysterically screaming into the telephone and making an ultimatum regarding lifting the blockade at the road on Ahmici. The (redacted) you referred to a moment ago, actually being aware of the importance of the moment, moved the receiver away from his head, so that we were able to hear directly what was coming out of the receiver. And as I said, very crude words were being used and very emphatic demands made, in the form of an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those words could be heard by all those present in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I assume they could. Perhaps not quite all of them, but quite a number of them, because that is the point. The (redacted) moved the receiver away from his ear, so that he could hear clearly all the words being spoken into the receiver, as well as a certain number of people in his vicinity could hear them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us not keep repeating. The person speaking into the telephone, could we agree that he was the person who could hear best the contents of the conversation with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, probably. It could be so, but not necessarily. But I do believe that he heard quite clearly what was being said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't quite understand why you said that that need not be so. Surely, if he is having the dialogue, he knows best what was said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I said that the named witness made a point of moving away the receiver from his head, holding it like this [indicates] in his hand, and he faced the rest of us, so that I couldn't be very precise about it, but judging -- I couldn't judge how he heard all the messages conveyed to him, but I do believe that he heard most of them. The reason why he moved away the receiver, as I said a moment ago, was because he wanted some other people to hear the messages being conveyed, in addition to himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, I think we have heard enough detail about this sequence. All you have to do is ask your client about this conversation, because he was on the phone. The witness is telling you the situation as he saw it, and I think, unless you are contesting something, that we have heard enough detail about it. You don't need to repeat the same question several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite agree, Your Honour. I was just going to end with this segment by making two statements. With the permission of the Court, I should like to draw attention to the witness to what Mr. Kovacic said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness who spoke to Mr. Kordic on the phone did not mention this ultimatum regarding the roadblock at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Not in a single word did he mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This has already been put. The witness affirms his recollection. I don't think there is much point going further with it. Is it denied that Mr. Kordic was involved in this? Is this evidence disputed on behalf of Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our position regarding this telephone conversation between Witness L and Mr. Kordic, we conveyed it on the 33rd day of the trial, on the 15th of June, on page 3.796, lines 2 to 8, when we stated what our position is clearly. I am just reminding you of that. But I would also like to say that Witness L, on page 6.854, towards the end of his testimony, stated explicitly what Mr. Kordic said, and our position is not substantially different from what Witness L said. So I think there is no need for us to debate this issue with this witness any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can remind us what you said on day 33, now it being day 110.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It is my mistake. Mr. Kordic said, roughly, to Witness L, that there would be no political negotiations until Refik Lendo ceases hostilities and does not assume his personal responsibility for the attack on HVO forces in Novi Travnik. So nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness AC, you've just heard what it is suggested that Dario Kordic said. Did he say something like that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This is just one aspect of what was discussed that night. It is possible that Witness L may have interpreted that as being the most important part of the conversation. As far as I am concerned, I abide by my testimony that I did indeed hear this part of the conversation that I mentioned in my testimony, that is, the ultimatum regarding lifting the roadblock at Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is up to Your Honours to adjudge on this issue, and I will not make any further questions, unless Your Honours have a question addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. AC, we can move on now. You said yesterday that Mr. Kordic, at the beginning of April 1993, issued some sort of an ultimatum for BiH army units to be attached and placed under the command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what context did he say that? Where did you hear him say it? On what occasion? Was it in writing? Could you tell us in greater detail about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This is something I heard on the radio, television of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the media, and it was broadcast on a number of occasions in local news programmes within the territory of Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt -- I apologise for interrupting you. So this was as a news item in the news, as a news report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Precisely. The context in which this ultimatum appeared had to do with the municipalities which were then formally within the so-called Herceg-Bosna; that is, the municipalities which were fictitiously within the composition of such an entity. The BiH army had to place itself under the command of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please. This news report, was it a lengthy report, or was it an isolated news item that was repeated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was in the media of Bosnia-Herzegovina in summary form. On the local media, it was broadcast in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was it ever stated where Mr. Kordic made this statement; at a meeting, at a gathering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The media I am referring to were under the competence of the HVO as well, because these were media that were designed to serve, among others, the HVO. And since such a message, or such an item was broadcast repeatedly, if there had been any kind of error, surely somebody would have intervened, because fully acknowledging the implications of such a message, surely we must agree that such a message is of very considerable significance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that this ultimatum was made orally and unofficially, that it was not official, and that is why no official reaction was expected on the part of the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant that the accused Kordic or any other institutions, which, in this case, could have taken any steps that this implied, did not address any kind of written request; nor did it address anyone in particular to whom that ultimatum was addressed. And that is why I described it as being unofficial, because when talking about members of the BiH army, it did not oblige anyone to make any kind of response.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I understand. But I still haven't received an answer from you whether, in those broadcasts, anyone said where Mr. Kordic had made this statement, and to whom. Had there been some kind of a meeting, a formal gathering or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There was no formal meeting. The accused Kordic and the command of the local HVO frequently used the local media to shape reports relating to the region to which those reports were addressed. So this report was broadcast on the local media in a way that said that the accused Kordic was behind this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This report that was repeated was read by professional announcers on the radio and the television, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I assume you are familiar with the Vance-Owen Plan and its provisions? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you must have also known about an order which the then Minister of Defence, Bozo Rajic, issued on the 15th of January, 1993, and which had to do with the attachment of the command of one of the army to the other, depending on the canton; that is, depending on which side had the majority in which canton?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Bozo Rajic? The Minister -- what was he?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of Herceg-Bosna and Bosnia-Herzegovina for some time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, at that time he was not the Minister of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you if you've heard about that order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that order. And I didn't find it in some other form, because what this order might imply was outside the context, and I did not think that that order had any particular significance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to show you D17/1.8, D17/1.8. This is an order which was based on the order that we've just talked about. Will you pay attention to the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an order issued by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, the head of the chief of staff, on the 15th of January, 1993. And on the basis of the order of Bozo Rajic, which I just mentioned, and some items of which explain in what provinces which army has to place itself under the command of the other side; that is, not only province number 10, that is, the Travnik region, but all the other provinces under the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must have seen it. See this date? It was January of 1993. Do you know this? Have you ever seen this order before, or at least do you know of the contents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, the document which was issued by the chief of staff of the HVO, and it says "confidential," but 21st of January, 1993 was the deadline. So this order, I should say, is insignificant from the point of view of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to conclude, all that you said on this particular topic is based on what you heard from the media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In this particular case, yes, but I should like to say the media which were controlled by the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not really want to put to you what other witnesses said except, Your Honours, to explain our position to you. In the beginning of April, or before or after, Mr. Kordic never issued such an ultimatum, and he had nothing to do with these attachment or subordination of various army units or, rather, placement of some army units under the command of other army units. He never had anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're coming to the close, Witness AC. You spoke about this plan, 48 Hours of Ashes, and I heard about it from you for the first time. If I understand properly, it should be the secret name, the code name of the operation. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, I believe I heard you well when you said that you received the first news about it from a member of the army of BH who had been in the Kaonik Prison before the 15th of April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I didn't hear you say how did he learn about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He was not from Vitez, Travnik, or Novi Travnik area. He came from a region which was further removed. And he had been an inmate there for quite some time, so that he had established contact with people, with guards who were in the prison compound, and I got this information from him. And let me explain. During that period of time, the man had never been out, so he could not have just come up with this term from some other source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was your information, and then -- and that is that the intelligence services that you already explained to Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to round off this topic, do you know the name of that soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I do -- I think about his lot. I know nothing about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment. Let me go through my notes. I believe that Mr. Cerkez's defence covered a considerable number of topics, and I don't have to go back to them. I believe I can conclude my cross-examination with this. Thank you very much for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to make two corrections with regard to what the Defence said; notably, Mr. Kovacic and then Mr. Naumovski a couple of minutes ago. It was said during the cross-examination that the witness mentioned the presence -- or, rather, Mr. Kajmovic did not mention the presence of the accused Mario Cerkez at that meeting on the 19th of October, 1992. This presence is confirmed by this witness in his testimony here, in the transcript, on page 3691. As for Mr. Naumovski, a moment ago he said that no witness mentioned the intervention of the accused Dario Kordic in the release of the detainees from the Kaonik in May 1993, and the witness was part of that. But there was another witness who was in that group, and he mentioned expressly as Kordic who had interceded, and it was on page 4393 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to have a dispute about this now. These matters can be argued in due course. Let's finish the witness's evidence. Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards that meeting, Witness AC, you were shown a document about the ceasefire on 7th of October, 1992, this ceasefire document, and that you saw the name Sulejman Kalco appearing there as one of those present as a signatory to this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Excuse me. That document -- you said that document had been shown to me. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is document Z246.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the witness could be shown it once again briefly. Z246.1. I can show it to the witness. I have it here. Perhaps it will be quicker if I do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a question about Marijan Skopljak and Mario Cerkez, but Marijan Skopljak does not appear on this document as a signatory to the document, but Mario Cerkez does.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sefkija Dzidic and Sulejman Kalco, in October 1992, were two persons responsible for the forces of the BH army in Vitez, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We really have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one more word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't get on with the case if there are constant interruptions. What is it, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor says Marijan Skopljak did not sign. Of course he didn't. He's not here. He said he's here. He's not listed. It's another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't worry about this. You can make your submissions in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have already asked you yesterday and I believe you answered it, but since you were cross-examined about it, we're going back to that. Witness AC, you know that in -- that every HVO Brigade and, after all, in the BH army brigade there were units, there are units of the military police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked if certain persons were taken to the chess club or to the SDK or the cinema -- and you spoke about that -- in order to protect them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked this morning. Do you have a feeling that on the 18th of April, in the morning, they came to look for you because they were concerned about your safety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I could never say that. We were all taken into custody against our wishes, and we were there also during -- and during our stay there, a number of people were victimised. I think about five persons. So I think it is absurd to speak about protection. Even where we were kept, people were being taken out and away to dig trenches and would not come back. That is, five persons were killed, and direct responsibility should be borne by those who were responsible for our accommodation in that facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us be clear. I mean, what I'm saying now, what I'm putting to you is not what I am putting in my own name; it is what came from the other side. Were there Vitez Croats who were in those same places as you were, in the cinema, in the chess club, or in the building of public auditing, or were they all only Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There were only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to seize this opportunity, Mr. President, to show you a document with regard to a document which Defence produced and which was tendered at the time when the witness and others were released on the 16th of May, 1993. We do not have an official translation of it, but we made an official request that an official translation be made of this document. This is a word "Croat" and the word "taken in" that is in the document but doesn't appear in the document. It is people who were taken or transferred, whereas the word "detained" or "arrested" would suit better. It is D29/2. And the last point, Mr. Witness. We spoke about Sadovace, the locality of Sadovace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Sadovace, is it a village with the Muslim population, but also Croats in the village of Sadovace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There were no Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last point which was raised by Mr. Naumovski just a moment ago. He spoke about an ultimatum on the 15th of January, '93, and you were shown a document, which I believe was issued by General Petkovic. Did you know, in the beginning of April '93, that the President of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, issued a similar ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: About that document, an ultimatum -- yes, I heard about it, but specifically referred to the area of Central Bosnia where we lived. The official thing about it was what was announced by public media, and behind it was the accused Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused Kordic. In the French version it said "Mario Cerkez." I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness AC, that concludes your evidence, and you are now released. Thank you very much for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You may now go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your patience, and I wish you plenty of success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, does this concern the witness at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does, but we don't need the witness. But if I may, I should like to respond to my learned friend. He said that I misinterpreted something. Just for the transcript, we do not need the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, briefly, because there is one other matter about the witness's evidence, and we need to get on with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. What it is that I want to say -- quite a series of questions that I asked of this witness, and the focus on the questions was the decision on the transfer of the whole group from Vitez to Busovaca, to the prison. And as far as I remember, no other witness spoke about it. So the transfer, that was at the focus of my question. That is all that I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, you raised during the examination a possibility of recalling Colonel Morsink to deal with Exhibit Z591, the list of the detainees in the cinema. In fact, the Trial Chamber has a suggestion about how this matter may be dealt with expeditiously, and I will ask Judge Bennouna to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lopez-Terres, very briefly, I think that instead of bringing back a witness for a very specific point, the authentication of a document, or for a statement regarding how that document was obtained, it is preferable, in our view, that this be done through a simple affidavit. And I think that your office has reminded us that we have admitted certain statements that you produced in a document that you sent to us on the 17th of January, 2000, as an affidavit. I am referring to a statement that you gave us to remind us of the affidavits of Mr. Lazarevic, which was translated from the Croatian, I think, and in which the person simply makes a statement; and there is a formula at the end, that this has been certified that Mr. Lazarevic has indeed signed this document, by his own hand, that his identity was established -- I am translating from the English -- on the basis of the fact that he is known by the officer who took the statement, and that this was done before the Municipality Court in Vitez. I don't know how one would translate that into French: the Municipal Court of Vitez. This type of statement, with regard to Mr. Morsink -- he must be Dutch, isn't he? I think it would -- then it would be even simpler to simply get a statement from him in -- before an authority, certifying this document. And in that case we wouldn't have to organise a fresh appearance of that witness. Rather, you could take care of it and address such a document to the Chamber. I am taking this opportunity to say that by sending this document to us, we see that it is possible before a Municipal Court in Vitez to have this type of affidavits, certified statements, or authenticated statements, without engaging in a cross-examination or the things that we were told before. This shows that this can be done, and this reminds us of the discussion we had previously on the question of affidavits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is up to me to thank you, Your Honour. The two documents you are referring to are documents coming from the procedure that you are familiar with -- not familiar with, regarding Kupreskic and others. Two affidavits, or formal statements, were produced by the Defence regarding the character of the various accused. And this is indeed something that we can think about, about using similar methods. Of course we have to act in accordance with the Dutch law, and we have to respect the local law, domestic law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for telling us that it was in the Kupreskic case, and these were statements regarding the character of the accused persons. Mr. Kovacic, you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honours. I wouldn't enter into this debate regarding the form of affidavits, whether it is possible in Bosnia or not, because, obviously, we will be discussing that at the Status Conference tomorrow, and we are preparing for it. But with regard to your proposition or your decision, if I can consider it a decision, for Mr. Morsink, instead of being called back, to be asked to make an affidavit. Of course I will abide by your ruling, but we would ask you to allow us, after, and depending on the contents of the affidavit, that we call him. Or it would be better for the Prosecutor to call him, because I doubt that he would react to an invitation by the Defence, except by a subpoena, which I think is unnecessary, that we be able to question him over certain circumstances. Your Honours, I have to be very cautious with that document, because I think you will understand, as this is the first document, and I claim that it is not truthful, but whereby the Prosecution is trying to produce evidence that the Vitez Brigade is directly linked to the detention of people in the cinema. You know my position. It was presented in our pre-trial brief. The only coincidence with the Vitez Brigade -- the only thing connecting the Vitez Brigade to detention is the fact that they were based in the same building. The Vitez Brigade has nothing to do with the detention in the cinema. That is our position. And this is the first piece of evidence relating to it. And if a witness comes and says, "I got this document," I have to be able to question him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I think that we have to view matters within their context, and to try and be sensible about things. We are going to ask Colonel Morsink, or, rather, the Prosecutor is going to ask Colonel Morsink how he obtained this document, under which circumstances he obtained it. As for the contents, and the arguments on substance, whether the Vitez Brigade was connected to the detention of these persons, that's another matter. And you can plead on that when the time comes. You have contested this document and its authenticity. You asked how it was obtained. The answer given was that it comes from Colonel Morsink, that he attached this document to his report. He is not present, because the question did not arise when he was present, so we are going to ask him how he obtained that document. And the Prosecutor is going to tell us in such-and-such a way. That is all. Now, if you wish to see Colonel Morsink, who is in the Netherlands, no doubt -- I forgot for a moment that we are in the Netherlands and that he is Dutch. And that is a fact, that this affects him, of course. But this is simply a sensible way of proceeding. We do not wish to have this person to testify on the contents itself; simply about the source of the document. I think that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is just one more problem in this connection. Yesterday I did not express myself correctly, saying that the document had not been disclosed. The Prosecution informed me kindly after the session that the document was disclosed, I think on the 14th or the 17th of December last year. That is much after Morsink came to testify. The document was not brought by Morsink. That is evident. Otherwise, it would have been disclosed to us earlier on. I don't know where the document came from, but it was disclosed to us. It is still on a pile in my office, which still hasn't been processed by me. That is why I said that it hasn't been disclosed, but I was corrected. The practical solution is obviously the one you suggest: for Morsink to make an affidavit. But, please, give me the right to recall him then, later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we have in mind your application. In due course we'll receive the affidavit, and then, if you've got submissions about it, of course we'll hear them then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it seems little point starting now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I agree. Can I use one of the five minutes to deal with a couple of points? First, there is no difficulty with the next witness coming back next week. As far as I understand from him, and I am sure that Victims and Witnesses Unit can arrange his travel to and from, so the fact that, inevitably, I think, he won't be finished this afternoon, does not present an insuperable problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we get through his evidence in chief --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- in that time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, how much time do you think you will need for the examination-in-chief of this witness, the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't yet know quite how much of the material is unchallenged. And I should draw to the Court's attention, and to my learned friends' attention, that the summary they were provided earlier has been amended in quite a number of places by the latest summary. The earlier summary was a draft, and there have been some additions and deletions and changes, so I don't know how much is going to be admitted, but I would have thought it will be about an hour and a half. That would be my guess. He's obviously a potentially very important witness, because he's got a lot of direct contact and direct knowledge. And my experience of him this morning is that he is not particularly expansive. He is not one of those witnesses who needs to be reined in. But, on the other hand, there is a limit to how far one can condense answers, when he is properly giving a full answer. I think about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We should aim to finish his evidence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will recall the exhibit under seal that was considered by a witness yesterday. 975,1 is the number. And I think that the position is that that document can only be shown to witnesses on a case-by-case basis, on the order of this Chamber. The Chamber might think that this is exactly the sort of witness to whom that document should be shown, because he has -- he's an on-the-ground commander at the time, knows exactly or is in a position to know exactly from his point of view what was happening, and I would seek leave for him to be shown that document, read it, in order to make comments on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered that, but you've already had one witness commenting on it, and we think that's enough. If there is a specific part you want to refer to, you can simply do it by asking the witness: Was it an attack on Ahmici? Whatever the report says, without referring to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To some degree, I've done that already this morning with the witness, but it hasn't found its way into the summary. I'm quite happy to deal with it that way. It possibly takes a little longer, but I'll be selective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And without referring specifically to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Chamber will recognise, from the questions that I ask, when I reach that point, that that's what I am doing and how I am doing it. And it may find it helpful to have the document at hand. Thank you very much. And as to next week, I've told my learned friends what the witnesses -- what the witness availability position is. I am pretty sure that with Merdan being part heard, we'll have a full week of evidence next week. Indeed, it may even prove to be quite difficult to squeeze it all in. And if we don't do that, we've got plenty of legal arguments that have got to be disposed of, sooner rather than later, particularly so far as the argument about Professor Cigar is concerned. And I very much hope that we can fit that in next week at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll aim to schedule that. We can do it tomorrow at. the Status Conference. Very well. Half past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness at some stage be provided with map 2781.2 as the map that may be of general use for reference when his evidence requires it. 2781.2. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Dzemal Merdan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Born in 1950, living in Busovaca until 1969, going to the national -- to the naval academy in Split and serving in the services from then on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By September 1991, what rank had you achieved in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The highest rank was Captain of the frigate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you return to Bosnia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice, on return to Bosnia, that there was redistribution of weapons to the Territorial Defence -- I mean, from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. From the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, weapons were being distributed to people of Serb nationality in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992, did you join the Territorial Defence, being based at the headquarters in Zenica? Were you then involved in planning and operations work in defence against the Serbs, becoming a commander of the Zenica Territorial Defence region?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes. In April 1992, I became a member of the headquarters for defence and then became a member of the Territorial Defence unit for the Zenica region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll deal with rank. What rank did you hold throughout 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At the time in the Territorial Defence, I did not have a rank. In 1992 there were no ranks in the Territorial Defence. But later on I received the rank of Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to complete that overall view of your personal history, have you stayed in the services since the conflict in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. From 1993, I was in the service of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presently holding the rank of?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Today I have the rank of Brigadier-General of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back, then, to 1992. Did you, in the course of your work, meet Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, Ignjac Kostroman, Pero Skopljak, Ivan Santic, Zoran Maric, Pero Krizanac, and Niko Grubesic on various occasions?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: That is correct. On different occasions I had occasion to meet the individuals that you have just enumerated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing first with Valenta: Did you see him in Vitez in the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him on several occasions in Vitez, and I saw him at the time you mentioned, once again in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at a public speech-making event, and if so, what, in a sentence, was his theme?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The people that you mentioned, I had occasion to listen to. I heard them speak. In concrete terms, Anto Valenta spoke in the hall in Vitez, and he spoke very negatively with respect to the relationships between Bosniaks and Croats in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his theme so far as Herceg-Bosna was concerned, and to whom that territory should belong?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In his speech, he stressed that Herceg-Bosna was a component part of the Republic of Croatia and that the aspirations of the Croatian people would be realised to live in a common state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At roughly the same time, did you see, not in the flesh, but a tape of Dario Kordic making a speech?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did see a tape in which Dario Kordic was speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His theme on the topic of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In one particular speech in the cultural centre in Busovaca. I think it was the beginning of 1992. I don't remember the exact date. It was a large rally to denote the victory of the HDZ. He spoke of Herceg-Bosna, and he said that the aspirations of the Croatian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be realised to live in one state, to live in the state of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A word about the HOS unit or units. Did such units exist in early 1992? Were they the same in all areas where they existed, if more than one?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in Central Bosnia -- that is to say, the zone of responsibility of which I was in charge -- HOS units did exist by a decision of the wartime presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't remember the exact date and the number of the order. It regulated that all units in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina be placed under the command of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the zone of responsibility of the Zenica region, the HOS unit of Zenica was placed under the command of the Territorial Defence, whereas the other HOS unit or other HOS units which were located in the area were not placed under the command of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before that, did HOS units in different areas have the same objectives or did they have differing objectives?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I can state for the HOS unit in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps -- that is to say, HOS Zenica, which executed orders -- and its goal was the same as the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, defence from the Serbian aggression. As to the other HOS units, I cannot comment on that, because they were not in the zone of responsibility under my command; that is to say, under the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the HOS unit that was under the command of the Territorial Defence of Zenica at the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: The HOS unit in the Zenica municipality was composed of the Croatian population from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Muslim population, that is to say Bosniaks from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when the global conflicts broke out, quite simply, it was extinguished; it disappeared. And part of the people of -- the Bosniaks, the Muslim religion, went to join the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas a portion, as far as I know, of the members of the HOS unit, who were of Croatian ethnicity, moved to the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Sarajevo airport negotiations at which Blaskic initially appeared, were you aware of those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I knew that negotiations were being conducted between the Territorial Defence, that is to say the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the representatives of the Serbs. And later on members of the Croatian Defence Council were included into those negotiations. And on the tape, the cassette, I saw that Blaskic promoted the interests of the Croatian Defence Council. After him, that was done by Dario Kordic. He advocated them. And I no longer saw Blaskic appear in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see any tape of how -- perhaps not a tape -- a media transmission of how Kordic introduced himself at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I had meetings with Kordic, where he introduced himself as Colonel of the HVO. And I saw him on tape. He also introduced himself as a Colonel of the HVO on these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn why Kordic had replaced Blaskic as the negotiator or spokesman?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I don't know the real reason, but I can only assume that Blaskic did not satisfy the demands of the Croatian Defence Council, because on several occasions Blaskic, as far as I know, was not able to make on-the-spot decisions, but this had to be done by Kordic. So I can only assume that that was the reason why Blaskic was replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We needn't trouble with paragraph 10. It's another list of names. Paragraph 11. Did you meet Cerkez on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never saw him involved in any direct wrongdoing, killing, or anything of that sort, did you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I did not see that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were his responsibilities at the time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: What I know is that Mario Cerkez was the commander of the HVO, in the Zenica municipality, and that he had a zone of responsibility in his municipality. I know for sure, and as a military man I am aware of the fact that commanders of units are responsible for the state of affairs in their zone of responsibility, and that they are duty-bound by their military duties to undertake adequate measures. And therefore I consider that, as a military man, Mario Cerkez is responsible for the zone of responsibility under his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in the course of that period of time, did those under his command, as you defined them, to your knowledge, engage in any activities that were not justified; and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Well, I can quote several cases, instances. The most grievous were the events in Ahmici and in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of your first statement, an organogram was prepared, not by you, but at the time of your making the statement. May the witness see that. It's the first of the series of exhibits. 2792. The whole stack can be distributed, if that's convenient. In fact, it's on the bottom of the stack. It's a document that looks like this. It's nearly at the bottom of the stack. This document, prepared in the case of your speaking to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, shows at the top Franjo Tudjman, and then Mate Boban, and then Dario Kordic. And then we see on the diagonal: Valenta, Kostroman, Skopljak. Then directly underneath Kordic we see a line, from the right to the left, Krizanac, Maric and Santic. Are those three political figures?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, they are political figures, as far as I know. I have in mind Pero Krizanac, Zoran Maric and Ivan Santic, when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I would just like to ask the Prosecutor to show us the source of the document, and when it was compiled, and by whom, so that we can follow this line of proceeding better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was prepared, as I understand it, by a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor in the course of discussions with this witness. So it's not physically his document. He didn't draw it. It was prepared at a time when he was discussing matters. And he's going to comment on it, qualify it and, as we shall see, eliminate from our consideration certain parts of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with those three political figures, did you, in your experience, find them to be responding to or subordinate to Kordic, in the way represented on this diagram?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I consider that they were responsible to Dario Kordic, and this they demonstrated on practice on several occasions, at least to the best of my knowledge and information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to the left, we have Furundzija and Darko Kraljevic. What do you say about their subordination to Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: For Darko Kraljevic, I can say that he was commander of the special forces in Vitez. And on several occasions I was witness to the fact that Blaskic was not able to command Darko Kraljevic, but somebody was always asked about this. And I think that somebody was Kordic. As for Anto Furundzija, I cannot make the same claims, because I am not acquainted with the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to the left, to the end of that line, there is a reference to Slobodan Praljak. Tell us about him.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Slobodan Praljak, I got to know in 1992. For the first time, I think it was in the month of October, or somewhere thereabouts. And I had a meeting with Mr. Praljak in Novi Travnik, and in Travnik. And during Christmas in Vitez, I think it was in 1992. I think that during the time Slobodan Praljak represented himself as the General of the Croatian army, that he wielded great influence in the system of leadership and command because he was able to exert pressure on Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The way the diagram appears has a line tracing down from "Praljak" through "Petkovic" to "Blaskic" and then on down. Does that reflect your view of the chain of authority or not? And notice, please, that off to the side of "Blaskic" and underneath "Petkovic" are "Ivica Rajic" and "Zeljko Siljeg."

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: In several occasions, in contact with Tihomir Blaskic, he told me that Milivoj Petkovic -- he told me that Milivoj Petkovic was his superior, and I had occasion to confirm this at two meetings that I was present, with the presence of Milivoj Petkovic as well. I think that was sufficient for me to realise that Milivoj Petkovic commanded Tihomir Blaskic at the time. As far as Zeljko Siljeg is concerned, I met him in 1992 in the office of Tihomir Blaskic at the Vitez Hotel in Vitez, and he was introduced as the commander of the zone of Prozor/Tomislavgrad. As far as Ivica Rajic is concerned, I met him at a meeting in Kiseljak. And I cannot claim that Milivoj Petkovic was directly in command of him as opposed to Tihomir Blaskic and Zeljko Siljeg. I consider that Milivoj Petkovic was in command of these two individuals at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going down that same line of authority, after "Franjo Nakic" we have a line of names: "Filipovic," "Krizanovic," "Cerkez," and "Nenad Santic." Is there a comment you want to make about the way they are positioned there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I can comment, yes. I know for sure that Franjo Nakic was the deputy of Tihomir Blaskic for the Operative Zone in that region, and that Filip Filipovic was, for a time, the commander of the brigade of the HVO in Travnik. I know that in that system of command Mario Cerkez was the commander of the HVO Brigade in Vitez. And here we need another direct link going up to Tihomir Blaskic, brigade commanders of the HVO of Busovaca, Zenica, Vares, Zepce, Usora. As far as Anto Krizanovic is concerned, and Nenad Santic, I think that they were in the chain of command under the command of Mario Cerkez in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there HVO at Novi Travnik as well?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot to mention the brigade of the HVO in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 12. What was your belief, on the basis of experience, of the relationship between Kordic and Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: On several occasions, I had occasion to see that Kordic had a great influence on Blaskic, and that in decisive moments when decisions were to be made, it was Dario Kordic who made the decisions, and that Tihomir Blaskic was to execute what Kordic had ordered him to do or told him to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Blaskic's behaviour when decisions had to be made at meetings involving HVO and the ABiH when he was on his own, he was unaccompanied? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Blaskic then asked to have consultations or he asked that the meeting be continued the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In early May 1992, was a meeting held at the Hotel Tisa in Busovaca? If so, can you tell us some of the senior HVO who were present?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. I don't remember the exact date, but it was May 1992. A meeting was held at the Tisa Hotel in Busovaca, and at that time the command post of the HVO at that meeting was Dario Kordic, Anto Sliskovic, Ignjac Kostroman, and I think Pasko was also there. Yes. Pasko was also there, but I can't remember his name, but it was Pasko. I know later on he became the chief of the military police in Vitez, because once when I happened to be arrested, he freed me in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed? What was the meeting about?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: They all wore military camouflage uniforms. The flashes, I believe they were the ones of the HVO. And we were talking about how to oppose the Serb aggression, but we could not find common language. We could not agree on that point because our views differed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On or about the 8th of May, was there an agreement concerning the local JNA barracks at Draga made, or indeed at Draga and Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: On the 8th of May, an agreement was reached about the barracks at Kaonik, and a little earlier an agreement on the barracks at Draga and at Silo were agreed. Those decisions of the war presidency of the municipality of Busovaca were not complied with, and were not complied with by Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the map will help, but if the witness has the map -- thank you. The Chamber, I know, will be acquainted with most of these places already, but the witness can, first of all, familiarise himself with the map so that he knows what it is he's looking at. The Chamber will know where Kaonik is for sure, and Kacuni, but it may be that Draga --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us a bit about that.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Draga is to the west of the village of Polje [indicates], opposite the road from Busovaca to Kacuni. If you're moving -- if you look from Busovaca to Kacuni, the Draga barracks was on the right-hand side, although they also had some area on the left-hand side. But all the facilities at the time were on the right-hand side of the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the Draga barracks compare in size with the Kacuni barracks?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: At a session of the war presidency in Busovaca, when the barracks at Draga and Silo -- rather, Kacuni -- were discussed, it was decided that the equipment of the former JNA should be divided between the Territorial Defence and the Croat Defence Council. However, this was not done, because the HVO, headed by Dario Kordic, entered the Draga barracks and allowed the TO to enter the Silo barracks at Kacuni. And at that news, we left the municipal hall in Busovaca and, headed by the chief of the municipality, Zoran Maric, who was also the president of the war presidency, we came to the barracks, and Dario Kordic would not allow us to enter the barracks. As for the facilities, I know it for a fact that the facilities at the Draga barracks number about 25 to 30, and in Kacuni, the barracks which we call the Silo, had only two facilities. I believe that Dario Kordic thought -- that is, I'm guessing -- that there was more materiel and equipment of the Yugoslav People's Army, and that's why he did what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, did the Territorial Defence go to Kaonik to get their supplies? In the event, what happened?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: I said that on the 8th of May an agreement had been reached at the war presidency of the Busovaca municipality. It was chaired by the president of the war presidency, Zoran Maric, and it was decided there that the equipment and materiel in the Kaonik barracks should be divided. On the basis of that, the president of the Territorial Defence set off to distribute that materiel. However, this vehicle, or vehicles -- I cannot remember. I think there were two vehicles -- but the first vehicle was intercepted in the area of Senduline Kuce and fire was opened on them by somebody from the HVO from a point. A member of the Croat Defence Council was severely wounded then, and a member of the Territorial Defence was inflicted some light injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, was an order issued by Dario Kordic for your arrest?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's already been tendered. 100. Exhibit 100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you held in the police station for two nights and then released?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your captivity, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: During my captivity, I was ill-treated, beaten, and I still suffer the consequences of it. They wanted me to order that the Territorial Defence surrender to the Croat Defence Council, and I refused that, because, true, I was the Territorial Defence commander, but the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina could decide about this surrender. I couldn't bear that responsibility as an individual. I could not surrender the units of the Territorial Defence to the Croat Defence Council. Then they were asking me about the situation in the barracks, what armaments they had, who was arming them, and so on and so forth. I fared very badly. In the morning, when Bruno came to see me, he told me that it had been ordered by Kordic; that is, that it was his order to arrest me and interrogate me. After that, I had an opportunity of seeing the order which said what Bruno had told me, and I attached a copy of this order to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The photographs, Your Honours, we'll find -- I think they are self-evident, which ones are the photographs. They are 2793,1 through to 6. If they could be made available to the witness. We can deal with them quite swiftly, although not so swiftly as to deny the technical booth the opportunity to focus on them for public display. But as soon as we've done that, we'll move to the next photograph, please, which is similar. What are the injuries shown there, please, Mr. Merdan? Anything shown on that photograph that you want to draw to our attention? The later ones are more obvious.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: On this photograph you can't see the injuries here. Those were pictures taken from the profile. I think these photographs were made some three or five days after my release. And I also had findings from the hospital, after I was released, but unfortunately I lost those findings, so I can't show it to the Court. Other photographs show it very clearly, what I looked like some four days after my release from prison. I need to mention here that the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina believe that a person who had received a very severe blow and has serious bruises, that the skin of a freshly slaughtered lamb should be applied to those injuries, and that is what they did. And that now this is the first time I am saying it, because a Croat from Busovaca, who slaughtered a lamb and gave him the hide so as to treat the wounds, the injuries inflicted on me by the Croat Defence Council. Will you please show other photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This photograph of your back --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: On this photograph one can see clearly the principal blows that were dealt to me, and I still suffer the consequences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following one has lines --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: This here is only from a different angle, but this photograph is made on the same day, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how those lines across your back --

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Yes. To the right, this is a major bruise, and when it is cold, it still turns blue. And I also have problems with my internal organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can the witness now, please, have two exhibits, which may be on the top of your stack. 101,1 and 101,2. Did you bring the originals of these two documents to Court today?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN
utterances.text: Let me see the second document, please. Yes, it is true; I brought the originals of these documents. These are the copies of the originals. The document that you can see on your monitors now is a document in which I declare that I will help the investigation which will be conducted, if it is proven that I am responsible for the events at Kaonik, in the barracks of Kaonik. And the second document, we see that it was signed by Anto Sliskovic for the regional headquarters, which was headed by Dario Kordic. It was again signed by Anto Sliskovic. I don't know why. The second document is the authorisation, the permit for my free movement through Herceg-Bosna, because I had some problems. I was arrested on several occasions. And on various occasions I tried to solve conflicts in Central Bosnia by peaceful means, or to prevent them from escalating. And that was why Dario Kordic issued me this authorisation, this free power for the territory of Herceg-Bosna, and I am in possession of the original of those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That first document, which you signed, why did you sign it? How did it come about that you signed it?
